scenario: During orientation, an IT security manager explains to a new staff member how secure areas use locks and swipe cards, enforce need-to-do access, require visitor accompaniment, ban items and activities like eating or smoking, and undergo periodic user access reviews to ensure only authorized personnel enter for valid business reasons.
expected_outcome: The new staff member understands the physical access controls for secure areas, including access restrictions, visitor policies, prohibited items and activities, and the process for periodic access reviews.
context:
21. Physical Access Controls
- All  visitors would be accompanied by an authorized IT person at all times during their stay inside the secure area.
- ITD would periodically review the list of users who have access to the secure areas and ensure that such access is granted to bona-fide individuals only.

21. Physical Access Controls
- ITD will designate certain areas of its infrastructure as ' Secure Areas ' .  This  will  include areas like Data Centre / Server Room / Communication Room.
- Secure  areas would be  protected by  appropriate  entry  controls  like  locks,  swipe  cards, proximity cards etc. to ensure that only authorized personnel are allowed access.
- Access to the secure areas would be limited to authorize users only.
- Access  permissions  to  the  secure  areas  would  be  granted  based  on ' need-to-do ' principle.
- Any  article  that  can  cause  threat  to  security  and  confidentiality  of  the  secure  areas  and/or  the  IT equipment installed therein would not be allowed inside the area.
- Appropriate security notices would be displayed inside and outside of the secure areas. Notices will also  be  displayed  prominently  inside  and  outside  the  secure  areas  prohibiting  eating,  drinking  and smoking inside the secure area.
- Visitors and temporary staff would be granted access to the secure area strictly on valid business purposes (e.g. maintenance, cleaning, audit etc.).

scenario: In a detailed IT meeting, the manager, backup admins, and asset owners debate defining backup frequency, types, and RTOs for diverse assets—like databases and firewall rules—while stressing same-day updates to backup procedures and secure storage methods that align with recovery time needs.
expected_outcome: The participants agree on backup frequencies, types, and RTOs for each asset, establish a process for same-day updates to backup procedures, and confirm secure storage methods aligned with recovery time requirements.
context:
Backup of Data
The  backup  requirements  would  be  formally  documented  and  be  made  available  to  all  backup administrators. Any changes to the backup process will be updated the same day the change has been approved.

Backup of Data
ITD  would  lay  down  processes  to  ensure  that  all  information  assets  of  the  Company  are backed up periodically and stored securely for retrieval when necessary.
The  asset  owners  are  responsible  for  defining  the  backup  requirements  of  the information  contained therein.    This    is    based on   the    availability    requirements    of    the  application  and  the  information contained therein. Examples of assets that will be considered are:
- Application databases
- System data (e.g. system files, application configuration files, source codes etc.)
- Development data (e.g. source codes, test database, test results etc)
- Firewall rulebase
- Router configuration files and Access Control Lists  ( ' ACLs ' )
The backup requirements would define the following:
Backup frequency (i.e. online, daily, weekly etc.),
Nature of backup (i.e. full backup, incremental backup),
Recovery   Time   Objective   ( ' RTO ' ,   i.e.   the   time   period   within   which   the information needs to be restored in the event of non-availability of the primary data).
The RTO would influence the manner in which the backup media is stored. For example, data with a very low RTO cannot be stored in an off-site location that is situated far away.

scenario: In a team meeting, a senior engineer imagines a sudden critical bug affecting Suspense boundaries and challenges beginners and the product manager to use React Developer Tools’ features—like toggling feature flags and visualizing state—to collaboratively diagnose and prioritize fixes under tight deadlines.
expected_outcome: The team agrees to use React Developer Tools collaboratively, leveraging each member's role-specific features to quickly diagnose and prioritize fixing the critical Suspense boundary bug.
context:
React Developer Tools caters to every role in a development team:

• Beginner – Visualise props and state without console.log.
• Product Manager – Toggle feature flags live to demo edge cases.
• Senior Engineer – Inspect Suspense boundaries, trace commits, and compare flame-graphs across branches.
• Performance Team – Export profiling data for regression tracking.

React Developer Tools equips your team with the visibility and control needed to maintain performance, debug complex issues, and understand component behavior. Whether you’re a beginner or part of a senior engineering team, this toolset is essential for scalable and maintainable React applications.

scenario: During a remote team meeting, a senior React developer explains React Developer Tools, then proposes a challenge: what if a sudden app update causes unexpected re-renders? They guide juniors through using the Profiler tab live to diagnose and fix these bottlenecks before the next release.
expected_outcome: The team learns how to use React Developer Tools, especially the Profiler tab, to identify and resolve unexpected re-renders, improving app performance before release.
context: React Developer Tools is an essential browser extension for React developers. It helps visualize components, inspect props and state, debug performance bottlenecks, and explore data-fetching logic—all without writing console.log statements. From beginners to performance teams, it provides powerful tools for building efficient apps.

React Developer Tools is your gateway to understanding your app’s live state and component structure.
🚀 Installation
• Chrome: React Developer Tools - Chrome Web Store
• Firefox: React Developer Tools - Firefox Add-ons
🧩 Components Tab
This tab shows all React components, props, state, and used context. For example, consider a Counter component:

```jsx
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Clicked {count} times</button>;
}
```
It renders real-time updates in the Components tab, removing the need for console logs.
🔥 Profiler Tab
The Profiler lets you record interactions, measure render times, and detect unnecessary re-renders. Example:

• Start recording
• Type into a search input
• Stop and review which components were rendered and why

This helps identify performance bottlenecks efficiently.
